question:
Patient note:
A 29-year-old woman with no significant past medical history walked into the urgent evaluation bay early this evening because her entire left lower limb had become “tight and huge” since yesterday morning. She recalls waking up for an early laboratory class, noticing that her favorite pair of skinny jeans would not slide up past mid-thigh on the left side, and assuming it was post-workout soreness from a light jog two days earlier. By lunchtime the same day she could see a visible difference between the two legs when seated at her desk, and climbing one flight of stairs to the anatomy lab caused a dull, throbbing discomfort that radiated from the medial calf toward the groin. She denies recent falls, twists, insect stings, penetrating injuries, or soft-tissue infections and has not noticed fevers, chills, night sweats, rigors, or weight change. There has been no chest pain, pleuritic discomfort, cough, dyspnea, palpitations, syncope, abdominal pain, or urinary complaints. She completed a 5 km charity run five days ago without incident and has maintained her usual routine of walking across campus between classes, stating that she has not required crutches, braces, casts, or walking boots at any point. She has never been diagnosed with clotting disorders, has no prior thromboembolic events, and takes no estrogen-containing contraception, glucocorticoids, or anticoagulants; her only medication is an as-needed ibuprofen tablet for menstrual cramps. There is no personal or first-degree family history of deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, premature myocardial infarction, or stroke, and she specifically denies malignancy, inflammatory bowel disease, nephrotic syndrome, or chronic heart failure. She has never been pregnant, does not smoke cigarettes, drinks wine socially once or twice per month, and has never used illicit substances. On arrival, before any therapeutic intervention, she appeared alert, oriented, and mildly uncomfortable when shifting position on the stretcher. Vital signs were temperature 37.0 °C, blood pressure 114/74 mm Hg, heart rate 94 beats/min and regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal S1 and S2 without murmurs, gallops, or rubs; lungs were clear on auscultation. The abdomen was soft, non-distended, and nontender with no palpable masses. Inspection of the lower extremities showed striking asymmetry: the left limb was globally enlarged from proximal thigh to ankle with a faint glossy sheen to the skin yet preserved normal color. Tape measurements taken 10 cm distal to the tibial tuberosity recorded a circumference of 45 cm on the symptomatic side versus 40 cm on the right, confirming a 5 cm discrepancy; at mid-thigh the left measured 56 cm and the right 51 cm. Palpation along the course of the common femoral vein in the inguinal crease, through the adductor canal, and across the popliteal fossa elicited localized tenderness most pronounced in the distal posterior thigh and upper calf, whereas similar pressure on the contralateral limb was painless. No palpable cords, fluctuance, crepitus, or masses were appreciated, and the skin temperature was marginally warmer over the tender track than over the right side. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses were 2 + bilaterally with brisk capillary refill; sensory examination to light touch and pinprick was intact, and motor strength graded 5/5 throughout both legs. Active and passive ranges of motion of the hip, knee, and ankle were full, though she winced slightly when the knee was flexed against resistance, correlating with the deep pathway discomfort. There were no varicosities, telangiectasias, or serpiginous superficial channels visible, and inguinal nodes were not enlarged. No erythematous streaks, bullae, or ulcerations were present, and Homan’s sign was not specifically elicited to avoid provoking unnecessary pain. Baseline laboratory testing obtained prior to any anticoagulation showed hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, platelet count 248 × 10⁹/L, leukocytes 6.9 × 10⁹/L, creatinine 0.82 mg/dL, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, INR 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 seconds; hepatic enzymes fell within reference limits. An electrocardiogram displayed normal sinus rhythm at 92 beats/min without ST-segment or T-wave abnormalities, and plain radiographs of the femur and tibia—ordered by the triage physician to exclude occult fracture—showed only soft-tissue fullness without osseous injury or gas. Given the abrupt onset of unilateral enlargement involving the entire length of the extremity, objective confirmation that the calf exceeds the contralateral side by more than 3 cm, focal tenderness precisely over the expected deep venous route, absence of a prior clotting history, lack of neurologic weakness or immobilization devices, and no competing infectious, traumatic, or orthopedic explanation on examination, an intraluminal obstruction within the deep venous system of the left lower limb is considered the leading concern, and duplex ultrasonography from the iliac segment to the ankle has been arranged on an urgent basis while therapeutic decisions await imaging confirmation.

Question: What is the patient's score of Wells' criteria for Deep Vein Thrombosis? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Wells DVT score assigns 1 point per positive DVT criterion and subtracts 2 if an alternative diagnosis is at least as likely.
- Entire left leg swollen from thigh to ankle: +1.
- Calf difference measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity: 45 − 40 = 5 cm, meeting the ≥3 cm criterion: +1.
- Localized tenderness along the femoral and popliteal deep veins: +1.
- Pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg is not documented: 0. No nonvaricose collateral superficial veins: 0.
- No active cancer, paralysis/paresis or lower-limb cast, recent bed rest of at least 3 days or major surgery within 12 weeks, or prior DVT: 0 each.
- No alternative diagnosis is at least as likely: 0 deduction.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.
Final answer: 3
